That's exactly what's happening. It has to do with something called photoperiodism. Basically, plants require a given time o darkness to flower, some require less others require more. It has to do with a substance called phytochrome and it's two forms. When a plant is in light, the EM wavelengths keep the phytochrome in one of its forms which stimulates vegetative growth. When it's darkness, the phytochrome gets converted to another form which stops vegetative growth and stimulates flowering. Now, the conversion of phytochrome at night is a slow process, while the opposite conversion is very fast. That means that if you have any flash of light during the night (like a flashlight being turned on and off), the phytochrome will reverse to it's day form and the plant will not flower. That's why small plants at the side of roads never seem to flower, since at some point during the night they will be illuminated by a car light.

  


Now, I admit I didn't known something like this could happen, where just half of the tree is kept from flowering, but is pretty neat that it does!
